newsitem.title: UK: Funds worried that "world equity party" over - poll.
newsitem.headline: Funds worried that "world equity party" over - poll.

text.p: Fund managers are concerned that rising short term interest rates will bring an end to the bull run in world equity markets, a Merrill Lynch survey said.
The poll by Gallup in early April said the move last month in the U.S. to raise Fed Funds rate by 25 basis points has had far-reaching effects.
"Fund managers around the world seem increasingly worried that rising short term interest rates will bring the world equity party to an abrupt end this year," the survey said.
It said two-thirds of U.S. fund managers expect further limited Fed activity and in the UK all of the managers surveyed said they expect base rates to rise in the coming year.
In Europe and Japan, there has been an increase in the number of managers expecting the central banks to tighten monetary policy.
But the survey said that instead of piling into cash, managers appeared to have become more selective in their country selection.
"The shift in investment intentions is visible in all the regions of our survey," it said.

Managers are keener to buy Japanese equities, and are less keen to increase their exposure to the Pacific Basin, reflecting the historic link between rising Fed Funds and falling equity prices in Hong Kong, and also the low correlation between Wall Street and the Nikkei.

The survey said the Fed rise had caused U.S. managers to become more bearish on the outlook for domestic equities, with bears outnumbering bulls by 37 percent on a three month view against 22 percent last month.
It said U.S. managers were net buyers of U.S. Treasury Bonds, and continued to look favourably on Latin American equities.

They were increased buyers of continental European and Japanese equities and net buyers of UK equities for the first time since the January survey. Demand for Pacific Basin equities was drying up, Merrill said.
Among sectors, U.S. managers were still favouring financials, with sentiment towards technology stocks easing further and utilities and building cyclicals least liked.
